To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

suboptimal posterior inference in variational inference is due to the limited capacity of the inference network and that the parameters used for increasing the expressiveness of approximating distributions play a role in improving the generalization of the inference network.

1) suboptimal inference in VAEs is often due to the amortization rather than the limited expressiveness of the approximating family; 2) this is due partly because the generator learns to compensate for the approximation, and partly because the parameters used to express the approximation play a more significant role in generalizing over data.

the parameters used for increasing the complexity of the approximator are used for generalizing inference over different data-points, and that the suboptimality of the inference is often due the amortization of the inference rather than the capacity of the approximating family.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
amortized inference is a double-edged sword, it allows for efficient inference but it can be suboptimal.
the quality of approximate inference in VAEs is largely determined by the capacity of the inference network and that the capacity of the approximation is a second-order factor.
the capacity of the variational approximation to model the true distribution is not the only factor that determines the quality of posterior inference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that amortized inference is a double edged sword: it is a powerful tool for scalable posterior approximation but can also lead to suboptimal inference.
the suboptimality in variational inference is often due not to a lack of complexity but to the difficulty of generalizing inference over all data points.
amortized inference is not a problem in itself but it can become a problem if it is not done carefully.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the quality of inference in VAEs can be improved by increasing the complexity of the recognition network, rather than increasing the complexity of variational distribution.
the recognition model can be trained to be more expressive, without increasing its capacity to generalize inference, by using a more expressive approximation.

the quality of approximate inference in variatical autoencoders is largely determined by how the generator is able to accommodate the choice approximation and the ability of the recognition network generalize over all data points.
